new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls by default on the final syllable (the survey-wide rule for all Mugil District languages, p. 734: 'The basic tendency is to stress the last syllable'; 'All genuine polysyllables are stressed on their last syllables'; verbal suffixes take the stress). Ate/Murupi departs from this in one morphologically defined class: polysyllables (chiefly inflected verb forms in -mi, e.g. maú-mi, dará-mi, abat-úmi, dó-mi, se'úmi) whose syllable count was increased by metathesis/assimilation of the original suffix are stressed on the penultimate; Em loans with unchanged syllable count keep final stress (uláy > uráy). Any non-final stress is marked with an acute in the wordlists (e.g. Ate vitúmi 'magic', p. 764).
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 734: 'Polysyllables formed by reduplication or compounding admit a secondary stress on the accented syllables of their components with the main stress, however, on the ultimate or penultimate respectively'; reduplicated monosyllables each keep their own stress (bén sór, bénsórsór).
new_statements.exceptions: (i) words with an unaccented suffix or postposition (-ik, -up, -ap, -yak, -ti, -to, -te, -we, -ne, -nge, -vo, -ga, -ho, -a, -ya, -way, -ey, -bara, -hon, -laten) keep stress on the base (amík-ta, alót-ip); (ii) lexical exceptions marked by acute (kalám vs amík); (iii) the Ate-specific penultimate class of metathesised verb forms; (iv) main stress reduced to a 'slur' after an interrogative particle and overridden by the sentence-final question suffix -e/-u.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, from questionnaire wordlists and phrases elicited c. 1930 by a missionary (Kaspruś had ~4 years' familiarity with Saker and Em; Ate data via 'good informants'); the general rule (p. 734) is stated for all Mugil District languages together (Austronesian Megiar/Matukar, Saker, and the Garus dialects Em, A'ẹ, Atẹ), the '1st Note' is the only Ate-specific stress statement. Non-final stress is marked with acute in the Atẹ vocabulary column (pp. 741-770). Kaspruś's 1946/49 errata (Anthropos 41/44: 370) leave the stress rules unchanged. No later source (Z'graggen 1971-1980 survey, Pick 2020, Glottolog) says anything about Murupi stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement is about Kaspruś's 'Atẹ' (Até) dialect of the 'Garus' group. Identification with Murupi [muru1273] rests on Z'graggen 1971: 30 (secs 2.21.12.18, 2.21.12.25: 'Kasprus's wordlist of Ate corresponds best to the author's wordlist collected on the Murupi language'; the area Kaspruś marked 'Ate' also contains Wamas [Z'graggen C12] and Lapting/Rapting [C11]), Z'graggen 1975b index ('Ate', 'Ate, Moek' = C14 Murupi), and Glottolog 5.1 attaching Kaspruś 1942/45 to muru1273. Kaspruś's Ate units (p. 726: Mo'ék, Asip, Vabit, Ibap, Vamias, Kimbis, Bai) include Murupi's village Bai and its alt name Moek but also Vamas (= Wamas). Z'graggen 1975b: 8 treats Wamas, Samosa, Murupi and Mosimo as one dialect chain (>81% shared vocabulary), so the statement may hold for that chain as a whole. Glottocodes of Wamas and Rapting not checked here.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Zero mentions of Murupi in the full text (a full-text search for stress/accent). Murupi is a Mabuso (Madang) language, not Northern Adelbert; the earlier scan's citation of Pick 2020 for Murupi was misapplied. Pick's stress section (1.5.1, pp. 31-32) concerns Mauwake, Pamosu, Usan only.
